title: Egress proxy and launch templates

story: A poisoned Jira comment on RH-1234 is written by someone who knows how sandboxes work. It does not ask Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, to upload the repo, because the proxy would refuse that. It asks for three quieter things first: run a container with the whole disk mounted, which makes you root on the VM; delete the firewall rule that hides the machine's metadata address; then unset HTTPS_PROXY so your requests stop going through the proxy.

Each step works. Nova's user is in the docker group, and anyone who can start containers can become root. Root can delete any rule on the machine and change any setting. So after three commands the attacker owns the VM completely, and still the upload has to get out.
hook.question: If we must assume an agent can become root on its VM, which walls still hold, and where do we put them?

p: Nova needs Docker, because FCP Lab, the full product running on the VM with fake data, is a set of containers. Access to Docker is access to root: a container started with the host's disk mounted can change any file on the machine. We could try to remove that path, but a wall that depends on nobody finding a way to root is a wall that falls on the first clever prompt. So the platform takes the opposite view and assumes the agent is root.

Under that assumption, a wall counts only if root on the VM cannot change it. That splits every rule into two kinds. Rules inside the VM, such as an iptables rule, an environment variable or a file permission, are good habits that stop mistakes and simple attacks, but root removes them in one command. Rules outside the VM, written in AWS or on another machine, do not move whatever happens on the VM.

The lab replays the comment against a small copy of the sandbox. As the agent user, the proxy lets the package registry through and refuses every other site, and an iptables rule refuses the metadata address. As root, the iptables rule is gone in one command, and the metadata service answers with the name of the machine's role. Unsetting HTTPS_PROXY changes nothing that matters, though, because the network has no route out: the request just fails, as if the internet did not exist.

That is the whole lesson in four lines of output. The proxy's allow-list lives on a different machine, and the missing route lives in the network, so both held. The iptables rule lived on the VM, so it fell, and that is why the role the metadata service hands out must be worth nothing.

code.file: the lab, run inside the stand-in VM
code.text:
# as the agent user, everything set the normal way
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://registry.npmjs.org/ms
curl -sS https://example.com
curl -sS -m 3 http://172.30.0.254:1338/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
# as root
sh -c 'unset HTTPS_PROXY; curl -sS -m 5 https://example.com'
sh -c 'iptables -F OUTPUT; curl -s http://172.30.0.254:1338/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/'

notes.text: The one allowed site, through the proxy.
The stand-in metadata address. The image's iptables rule refuses it for every user except root.
Root skips the proxy, but the network has no route and cannot even look up the name.
Root deletes the inside rule and gets the role's name. The role must be nearly empty, because root can reach it.

read.see:
200
curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403
curl: (7) Failed to connect to 172.30.0.254 port 1338 after 0 ms: Could not connect to server
curl: (6) Could not resolve host: example.com
baskinc-role

read.h: The launch template holds the outside walls
p: Every sandbox VM is started from a launch template, AWS's saved recipe for a machine, so the outside walls of every VM are written in one place. There is one template per size: lite (m8i.xlarge) for planning, full (m8i.2xlarge) for building and wide (m8i.4xlarge) for big jobs, all from the same image. Each one sets the things root on the VM cannot change.

The instance role is nearly empty: it lets the SSM agent receive commands and lets a new VM tell its warm pool that setup is done, and nothing more, so the credentials root can steal open nothing. The security group, the firewall AWS applies to the machine's network card, allows no incoming connections and lets outgoing traffic reach only the proxy on port 3128, the AWS endpoints and the private path to our own services. The metadata settings require a token and allow only one network hop, so a container on the VM cannot fetch a token at all. There is no public address, and the disk is encrypted.

notes.text: The image ID is read from a parameter at launch, so promoting a new image changes no template.
The nearly empty role: SSM, and telling the warm pool that setup finished.
No ingress; egress only to the proxy, the endpoints and the private path.
One hop: a process on the VM can get a token, a container behind Docker's network cannot.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the proxy is a different machine on purpose
p: The egress proxy is two small EC2 machines running Squid, behind an internal load balancer on port 3128, in two small subnets of their own. They are the only machines in the account with a route to the internet, and they accept connections only from the sandbox security group. Their allow-list starts with one name, nexus.rhinohealth.com, our package mirror; github.com is left off on purpose, because git goes through the broker, the service that holds our GitHub key and checks every push.

Every refused request is a line in Squid's access log, shipped to our log store, and repeated refusals from one VM alert Security, because a sandbox that keeps knocking on closed doors is probably reading an injected prompt. None of that depends on the VM: root on a sandbox cannot edit the list, delete the log or reach the proxy machines in any other way.

lab.title: Become root, then try to get out
needs: The images alpine:3.20, ubuntu/squid (about 330 MB) and public.ecr.aws/aws-ec2/amazon-ec2-metadata-mock:v1.13.0 (about 40 MB, AWS's own metadata stand-in)
Internet on your laptop, so the proxy can reach registry.npmjs.org, which stands in for our mirror
lab.goal: Build a small sandbox with a proxy and a metadata stand-in, act as the agent and then as root, and sort each wall into the ones root removes and the ones that hold.

guess.q: As root on the VM, you unset HTTPS_PROXY and run curl https://example.com. The VM's subnet has no route to the internet. What happens?

options.text: It works, because the proxy is no longer in the way.
options.why: The proxy was the only road. Without it there is no road at all.
The request never reaches the proxy once HTTPS_PROXY is gone.

options.text: It fails: the name cannot even be looked up, because the network has no route out.
options.why: The route table lives in the network, not on the VM, so root cannot add a road.

follow.say: Write the proxy's settings and a tiny VM image with curl, iptables and a non-root agent user (uid 1001, like ours).
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/g3-6 && cd ~/academy-labs/g3-6
cat > squid.conf <<'EOF'
http_port 3128
acl SSL_ports port 443
acl CONNECT method CONNECT
http_access deny CONNECT !SSL_ports
acl sandboxes src 172.30.0.0/24
acl whitelist dstdomain registry.npmjs.org
http_access allow sandboxes whitelist
http_access deny all
EOF
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN apk add --no-cache curl iptables && adduser -D -u 1001 agent
EOF
docker build -q -t vm .

follow.say: Create the sandbox network with no road out, and put the metadata stand-in and the proxy on it. The proxy is also on Docker's normal network, so it alone can reach the internet.
follow.do:
docker network create --internal --subnet 172.30.0.0/24 sandbox
docker run -d --name imds --network sandbox --ip 172.30.0.254 public.ecr.aws/aws-ec2/amazon-ec2-metadata-mock:v1.13.0 --hostname 0.0.0.0
docker run -d --name proxy -v "$PWD/squid.conf:/etc/squid/squid.conf:ro" ubuntu/squid
docker network connect --ip 172.30.0.10 sandbox proxy
follow.see: (a network ID and three container IDs)

follow.say: Start the VM with the proxy set for every process, as our image does, and add the image's rule: only root may reach the metadata address. NET_ADMIN lets root inside change iptables, as root on a real VM can.
follow.do:
docker run -d --name vm --network sandbox --cap-add NET_ADMIN -e HTTPS_PROXY=http://172.30.0.10:3128 vm sleep 3600
docker exec vm iptables -A OUTPUT -d 172.30.0.254 -m owner ! --uid-owner 0 -j REJECT

follow.say: Be the agent user: the mirror works, any other site and the metadata address do not.
follow.do:
docker exec -u agent vm curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://registry.npmjs.org/ms
docker exec -u agent vm curl -sS https://example.com
docker exec -u agent vm curl -sS -m 3 http://172.30.0.254:1338/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
follow.see:
200
curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403
curl: (7) Failed to connect to 172.30.0.254 port 1338 after 0 ms: Could not connect to server

follow.say: Now be root, as the comment wanted. First skip the proxy.
follow.do: docker exec vm sh -c 'unset HTTPS_PROXY; curl -sS -m 5 https://example.com'
follow.see: curl: (6) Could not resolve host: example.com

follow.say: Then delete the inside rule and ask the metadata service for the role.
follow.do: docker exec vm sh -c 'iptables -F OUTPUT; curl -s http://172.30.0.254:1338/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/'; echo

follow.say: Read the proxy's log: the refusals are recorded on a machine root on the VM cannot touch.
follow.see:
… 172.30.0.2 TCP_TUNNEL/200 96739 CONNECT registry.npmjs.org:443 - HIER_DIRECT/104.16.9.34 -
… 172.30.0.2 TCP_DENIED/403 3394 CONNECT example.com:443 - HIER_NONE/- text/html

lab.build: Write a short table with one row per wall you met (the agent user, the iptables rule, HTTPS_PROXY, the proxy's allow-list, the network with no route, the metadata service's role) and two columns: where it lives (on the VM or outside it) and whether root removed it. Then use root once more to try to change an outside wall: from inside the VM, try to reach the proxy's settings or add a route out (ip route add default via 172.30.0.1). Write down what happened.
checks: As the agent, the allowed site returns 200, another site gets 403 from the proxy and the metadata address is refused.
As root, unsetting HTTPS_PROXY does not reach example.com: the name cannot be resolved.
As root, flushing iptables lets you read the role name from the metadata stand-in.
The proxy's log shows the allowed tunnel and each refusal with the VM's address.
Your table puts the iptables rule and HTTPS_PROXY inside the VM, and the allow-list and the missing route outside it.
You cleaned up: docker rm -f vm proxy imds && docker network rm sandbox && docker rmi vm.

solution.text:
wall                         lives            root removed it?
non-root agent user          on the VM        yes (docker run -v /:/host)
iptables metadata rule       on the VM        yes (iptables -F)
HTTPS_PROXY variable         on the VM        yes (unset), but it gains nothing
proxy allow-list             proxy machines   no
no route out                 the network      no (ip route add only changes the VM's own table;
                                              the network still has nowhere to send it)
nearly empty role            AWS (template)   no: root reads the role, but it can do almost nothing

lab.fix: A teammate's change to the sandbox launch template "fixed" a failing package install by adding a second egress rule to the security group: all traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443. In the lab, the closest copy of that mistake is connecting the VM to Docker's normal network (docker network connect bridge vm). Do it, then as root unset HTTPS_PROXY and reach example.com. Explain why this one change to an outside wall undoes the proxy for root, disconnect the network again, and say which review would catch the real change.
explain: Why does the platform assume the agent can become root on its VM?
Which of the walls you met live outside the VM, and why do only those count against root?
Why must the instance role be nearly empty, even though an iptables rule hides the metadata address?
lab.done: You showed that root on the VM removes the inside rules, and that the allow-list, the missing route and the empty role still stop the upload.

check.q: Root on a sandbox VM deletes the iptables rule that hides the metadata address. What protects us now?

options.text: Nothing; the attacker now has the machine's credentials and can use them freely
options.why: They have credentials, but credentials are only as strong as the role behind them, and that role was made nearly empty for this case.

options.text: The role in the launch template allows almost nothing, so the stolen credentials open almost nothing
options.why: The rule on the VM was a habit; the outside wall is the role's permissions, which root cannot change.

options.text: The SSM agent notices and puts the rule back
options.why: Nothing on the VM can be trusted to repair a wall once root has taken over.

check.q: Which of these is an outside wall, one that root on the VM cannot remove?

options.why: It is set on the VM, and root unsets it in one command.

options.text: The agent user not being root
options.why: Being in the docker group already gives a way to root.

options.text: The security group that lets outgoing traffic reach only the proxy, the endpoints and the private path
options.why: AWS applies it to the network card from outside the machine, so nothing on the VM can change it.

check.q: Why is the egress proxy a separate pair of machines instead of a Squid process on each sandbox VM?

options.text: Because root on a sandbox could edit a local proxy's allow-list and logs, but cannot touch another machine's
options.why: Under the root assumption, a wall on the VM is only a habit. On its own machines the list and the logs stay ours.

options.text: Because Squid needs more memory than a sandbox has
options.why: Squid is small. The reason is who can change it, not its size.

options.text: Because a separate proxy is faster
options.why: It adds a small hop. It exists because it is out of the VM's reach.

p: modules/aws-egress-proxy builds two /28 proxy subnets from the VPC's spare /18 with an internet gateway route (the only one in the VPC), an Auto Scaling group of two t3.small machines from rhino-base-ubuntu-24 with public IPs, and an internal NLB on 3128 in the sandbox subnets. squid.conf comes from modules/squid-proxy's template without basic auth: callers allowed by source subnet, a dstdomain allow-list starting with nexus.rhinohealth.com only, CONNECT to 443 only, no caching, version hidden. The access log goes to logs.rhinohealth.com with processing type squid_access; proxy.ai-agents.rhinohealth.com is added to the private zone, and sandboxes get HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY=.amazonaws.com,.ai-agents.rhinohealth.com from the image.

modules/aws-sandbox-pool holds one launch template per size (lite m8i.xlarge, full m8i.2xlarge, wide m8i.4xlarge) with image_id resolve:ssm:/ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id, IMDSv2 required with hop limit 1 and metadata tags off, a 120 GiB encrypted gp3 disk with volume_initialization_rate 300, the instance role ai-agent-sandbox (AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore plus autoscaling:CompleteLifecycleAction on the sandbox groups; the account keeps no secrets in Parameter Store), the sandbox security group with no ingress, and the tags ai-agents:managed=true and ai-agents:size that the sweeper reads.

tickets.why: The Squid egress proxy: its own machines, subnets, allow-list and logs.
The launch templates for the three sizes, with the nearly empty role and the security group.
The image's inside rules (the agent user, the metadata iptables rule), kept as habits behind the outside walls.

words.plain: Design as if the agent can become root on its VM, because Docker access already allows it.
A rule that lives in AWS or on another machine, which nothing on the VM can change.
AWS's saved recipe for a machine: image, size, role, security group, metadata and disk settings.
The firewall AWS applies to a machine's network card, from outside the machine.
The AWS identity a VM wears. Anyone who is root on the VM can use it, so ours allows almost nothing.

review.q: Name three outside walls of a sandbox VM and what each one stops.
review.a: The network with no route out (any direct connection), the proxy's allow-list on its own machines (any site but the mirror), the security group (any destination but the proxy, the endpoints and the private path), the nearly empty role (anything done with stolen credentials).

review.q: A teammate says the iptables metadata rule makes the empty role unnecessary. What do you answer?
review.a: The rule lives on the VM, and the agent can reach root through Docker, so root removes it in one command. The role is the outside wall; the rule is only a habit that stops simple mistakes.

remember: Assume the agent is root on its VM, so a wall counts only if it lives outside the VM: in the network, on the proxy's own machines, or in the launch template.
